# Filtering Light Pollution from a Starfield

<a class="gallery-back" href="../gallery.qmd">← Back to Gallery</a>

**Topic:** Filter design in two dimensions — separating a smooth light-pollution gradient from point-like stars by where they live in the spatial-frequency plane.
**Chapter:** [6 — Signal Processing](../chap6.qmd)

---

## Background

Anyone who has pointed a camera at the night sky from a city knows the problem: instead of a black background peppered with stars, you get a bright, uneven wash of orange **skyglow** — sunlight's nighttime cousin, scattered back down by streetlights and haze. It swamps the faint stars and tilts the whole frame brighter on the side facing the city.

The saving grace is that **skyglow and stars occupy completely different spatial scales.** Light pollution is a *smooth* gradient — it varies gently across the entire frame, so all of its energy sits at very **low spatial frequencies**. A star, by contrast, is a near-point source: a sharp spike a couple of pixels wide, which spreads its energy across **high spatial frequencies**. This is the two-dimensional version of the everyday filtering problem from [Chapter 6](../chap6.qmd) — a slow drift riding under a fast signal — and the same tool applies: build a filter that keeps one frequency band and rejects the other.

## Key idea

Take the 2-D FFT of the frame and the two components fall into different places: the skyglow piles up in a tight blob around the origin ($\mathbf k \approx 0$), while the stars scatter power out to the edges. So the **filter design is a high-pass**:

1. Estimate the background by keeping only the low-frequency core — multiply the spectrum by a smooth Gaussian **low-pass** $e^{-k^2/2k_c^2}$ and transform back. That reconstructs the skyglow alone.
2. **Subtract** it. What remains is the high-pass residual: stars on a flat, near-black sky.

Choosing the cutoff $k_c$ is the whole craft, exactly as when picking a 1-D filter's corner frequency. Too high and you start eating the stars' wings and any real extended nebulosity; too low and the gradient leaks through. One subtlety carries over from 1-D filtering too: a periodic FFT treats opposite edges as neighbours, so a frame that is brighter on one side than the other has a discontinuity at the wrap-around — left unhandled it rings along the borders. Padding the image with a mirror reflection before transforming removes that seam, the 2-D analogue of windowing.

## Code

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter

# polluted = starfield  +  smooth skyglow gradient  +  noise   (a 512x512 frame)
kc  = 0.010                                        # cutoff spatial frequency [cycles/pixel]
pad = polluted.shape[0] // 2

# reflect-pad so the periodic FFT sees no brightness jump at the edges (no ringing)
P  = np.pad(polluted, pad, mode='reflect'); M = P.shape[0]
kx = np.fft.fftfreq(M); KX, KY = np.meshgrid(kx, kx)
lowpass = np.exp(-(KX**2 + KY**2) / (2 * kc**2))   # smooth 2-D low-pass = background model

background = np.real(np.fft.ifft2(np.fft.fft2(P) * lowpass))[pad:-pad, pad:-pad]
cleaned    = polluted - background                 # high-pass: skyglow removed, stars kept
```

## Result

<div class="gallery-result">
![Four panels. (a) A synthetic light-polluted frame: faint stars buried under a bright skyglow gradient from a city near one corner. (b) Its 2-D spatial-frequency spectrum (Hann-windowed for display) — the skyglow's energy is concentrated in the bright low-k core inside the dashed circle, while star energy fills the rest of the plane. (c) The low-pass reconstruction of that core: the smooth skyglow the filter identifies and removes. (d) The high-pass result — the same stars on a flat, dark sky.](../Figure/figure_light_pollution.png)
</div>

Panel (b) is why this works at all: the light pollution collapses into the bright core at the centre of the frequency plane, cleanly separated from the star field that fills the rest. The Gaussian low-pass (dashed circle) scoops out just that core to build the **skyglow model** in panel (c) — a smooth surface that traces the city-glow gradient and its corner hotspot, with no stars in it. Subtracting it leaves panel (d): the background flattens (its standard deviation drops about five-fold here) and stars that were invisible under the glow now stand out against a dark sky.

The example also shows the method's honest limit. Genuinely *extended* structure — the faint patch of nebulosity in the lower-right — lives at low spatial frequencies too, so it is partly swept into the background model and dimmed along with the skyglow. That is the same trade-off a 1-D high-pass makes when a signal and its baseline drift overlap in frequency, and it is why astrophotographers reach for gentler cutoffs, masked background models, or wavelet-based tools when they want to preserve nebulosity. Choosing where to cut is the filter design.
